content: Mefenamic acid is expected to be excreted into human breast milk based on its physical and chemical properties. Metabolism: Mefenamic acid is metabolized by the cytochrome P450 enzyme CYP2C9 into 3-hydroxymethyl mefenamic acid (Metabolite I). The activity of these metabolites has not been studied. These metabolites may undergo glucuronidation, and mefenamic acid itself is also directly glucuronidated. After a single 1-gram dose, a peak plasma level of approximately 20 mcg/mL was observed at 3 hours for the hydroxy metabolite and its glucuronide (n=6). Excretion: Approximately 52% of a mefenamic acid dose is excreted in the urine, primarily as glucuronides of mefenamic acid (6%), 3-hydroxymefenamic acid (25%), and 3-carboxymefenamic acid (21%). The elimination half-life of mefenamic acid is approximately two hours. Metabolites may accumulate in patients with renal or hepatic failure. The mefenamic acid glucuronide may irreversibly bind to plasma proteins. Since both renal and hepatic excretion are significant pathways for elimination, dosage adjustments may be necessary in patients with renal or hepatic dysfunction. Mefenamic acid should not be administered to patients with preexisting renal disease or significantly impaired renal function. Special Populations: Pediatric: Mefenamic acid has not been adequately studied in pediatric patients under 14 years of age. A study in 17 preterm infants administered 2 mg/kg indicated that the half-life was about five times longer than in adults, consistent with the low activity of metabolic enzymes in newborns. The mean time to maximum concentration (Tmax) was 8 hours (range: 2 to 18 hours). Race: No pharmacokinetic differences due to race have been identified. Hepatic Insufficiency: The pharmacokinetics of mefenamic acid have not been studied in patients with hepatic dysfunction. Since hepatic metabolism is a significant pathway for mefenamic acid elimination, patients with acute or chronic hepatic disease may require reduced doses compared to those with normal hepatic function. Renal Insufficiency: The pharmacokinetics of mefenamic acid have not been investigated in patients with renal insufficiency. Given that mefenamic acid, its metabolites, and conjugates are primarily excreted by the kidneys, there is potential for metabolite accumulation. Mefenamic acid should not be administered to patients with preexisting renal disease or significantly impaired renal function. Clinical Studies: In controlled, double-blind clinical trials, mefenamic acid was evaluated for the treatment of primary spasmodic dysmenorrhea. Efficacy parameters included pain assessment by both patients and investigators, the need for concurrent analgesic medication, and evaluation of changes in the frequency and severity of symptoms characteristic of spasmodic dysmenorrhea. Patients received either mefenamic acid, 500 mg (2 capsules) as an initial dose followed by 250 mg every 6 hours, or placebo at the onset of bleeding or pain, whichever began first. After three menstrual cycles, patients were crossed over to the alternate treatment for an additional three cycles. Mefenamic acid was significantly superior to placebo in all parameters, and both treatments (drug and placebo) were equally well tolerated. Nonclinical Toxicology: There is limited information regarding the nonclinical toxicology of mefenamic acid in the drug label. How Supplied: Mefenamic Acid Capsules USP 250 mg are size ‘1’ yellow-yellow capsules with ‘PAD’ imprinted on the cap and ‘195’ imprinted on the body. They are supplied as follows: Bottles of 30: NDC 0574-0195-30 Bottles of 100: NDC 0574-0195-01 Storage: Store at 20-25°C (68-77°F); excursions permitted to 15-30°C (59-86°F). Patient Counseling Information: Patients should be informed of the following before initiating therapy with an NSAID and periodically during ongoing therapy. They should also be encouraged to read the NSAID Medication Guide accompanying each prescription dispensed. Mefenamic acid, like other NSAIDs, may cause serious cardiovascular side effects, such as myocardial infarction (MI) or stroke, which may result in hospitalization or death. Although serious cardiovascular events can occur without warning symptoms, patients should be alert for signs and symptoms such as chest pain, shortness of breath, weakness, or slurring of speech, and seek medical advice if any indicative signs or symptoms are observed. Mefenamic acid, like other NSAIDs, can cause gastrointestinal (GI) discomfort and, rarely, serious GI side effects such as ulcers and bleeding, which may result in hospitalization or death. Although serious GI tract ulcerations and bleeding can occur without warning symptoms, patients should be alert for signs and symptoms such as epigastric pain, dyspepsia, melena, or hematemesis, and seek medical advice if any indicative signs or symptoms are observed. Mefenamic acid, like other NSAIDs, can cause serious skin side effects such as exfoliative dermatitis, Stevens-Johnson syndrome (SJS), and toxic epidermal necrolysis (TEN), which may result in hospitalization or death. Although serious skin reactions may occur without warning, patients should be alert for signs and symptoms such as skin rash, blisters, fever, or other signs of hypersensitivity such as itching, and seek medical advice if any indicative signs or symptoms are observed.
